title: ASP.NET Core and EF Core
blurb: DI lifetimes, the middleware pipeline, model binding, configuration, EF Core. The two most reliably asked .NET interview questions live in here.

questions.q: What is the difference between Singleton, Scoped and Transient?
choices: Singleton: one for the app's lifetime. Scoped: one per request. Transient: a new one every time it is resolved
They control how long an object stays in memory before GC
Singleton is per request, Scoped is per application
questions.why: DbContext is scoped because it tracks changes for one unit of work. Stateless helpers can be singletons. Transient is the safe default for cheap objects with no shared state.
questions.asked: The single most asked .NET interview question. Know it cold.

questions.q: What is a captive dependency?
choices: A longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one — e.g. a singleton capturing a scoped DbContext
A circular dependency between two services
A service resolved outside the container
questions.why: The scoped object is captured on first resolution and then reused for the life of the singleton — so one DbContext is shared across every request, which is neither thread-safe nor correct. Inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work.
questions.asked: The natural depth follow-up to the lifetimes question, and it separates real experience from memorisation.

questions.q: Why does the order of `app.Use...` calls matter?
choices: Middleware forms an ordered pipeline; each component can short-circuit or pass to the next
It does not matter — ASP.NET Core sorts them
Only the first and last matter
questions.why: UseAuthentication must come before UseAuthorization, both must come before endpoints, and UseCors must come before anything that would short-circuit the preflight. Wrong order usually fails silently rather than crashing.
questions.asked: The second most asked .NET question. Expect to be asked to place a few in order.

questions.q: How does a middleware short-circuit the pipeline?
choices: By writing a response and not calling `await next(context)`
questions.why: That is how authorisation returns 401 without ever reaching your endpoint, and how a caching middleware serves a hit. Calling next after writing the response is a common bug — headers are already sent.

questions.q: Where does ASP.NET Core read configuration from, and in what order?
choices: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, then user secrets, then environment variables, then command line — later wins
questions.why: Later providers override earlier ones, which is exactly what lets a container override a file value with an environment variable. Nested keys use `Section__Key` in environment variables.

questions.q: What is the difference between `IOptions<T>`, `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` and `IOptionsMonitor<T>`?
choices: IOptions is a singleton read once; IOptionsSnapshot is scoped and re-reads per request; IOptionsMonitor supports change notifications
questions.why: If a config change should take effect without a restart, IOptions will not see it. Note IOptionsSnapshot cannot be injected into a singleton — that is a captive dependency.

questions.q: Where do model validation errors surface in a controller-based API?
choices: `[ApiController]` automatically returns a 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body before your action runs
You must check ModelState.IsValid manually in every action
questions.why: With `[ApiController]` the automatic 400 happens for you. Without the attribute — or in a minimal API — you check yourself. Knowing which applies is what the question is testing.

questions.q: What is model binding?
choices: Mapping route values, query string, headers and body onto action parameters and their types
Binding a view to a model
Mapping an entity to a database table
questions.why: The bug it causes: a complex type binds from the body by default, a simple type from the route or query. Getting a null parameter usually means the source is not where the binder looked — hence `[FromBody]`, `[FromQuery]`.

questions.q: What is ProblemDetails?
choices: The RFC 7807 standard error body — type, title, status, detail, and optional field errors
questions.why: Using the standard shape means clients and tooling can parse errors without bespoke code. Wire it up in one exception-handling middleware rather than try/catch in every action.

questions.q: What does EF Core's change tracker do?
choices: Records the original values of loaded entities so SaveChanges can generate the right UPDATE statements
questions.why: It is why you can mutate an entity and call SaveChanges with no explicit update. For read-only queries `AsNoTracking()` skips the bookkeeping and is meaningfully faster on large result sets.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always AsNoTracking — an easy, concrete performance win to mention.

questions.q: What causes an N+1 in EF Core, and how do you fix it?
choices: Accessing a navigation property per row — fix with Include, a projection, or split queries
questions.why: `Include` eagerly joins. A `Select` projection into a DTO is often better — it fetches only the columns you need. Log the generated SQL in development so you can actually see it happening.

questions.q: Why is DbContext registered as Scoped?
choices: It is not thread-safe and represents one unit of work per request
Because it is expensive to construct
To keep the connection open across requests
Because EF Core requires it for migrations
questions.why: Two concurrent requests sharing a context would corrupt the change tracker. For background work you create your own scope — you cannot inject the request-scoped one into a singleton.

questions.q: What is a migration in EF Core?
choices: A generated, checked-in C# class describing a schema change, applied in order to bring a database up to date
A change to the model classes only
questions.why: `dotnet ef migrations add` scaffolds it from model changes; `database update` applies it. In production, applying migrations automatically at startup is convenient and risky — a failed migration takes the app down and multiple instances race.

questions.q: What is the difference between a minimal API and a controller-based API?
choices: Minimal APIs map endpoints directly with less ceremony; controllers give conventions, filters and attribute routing
Minimal APIs cannot use dependency injection
questions.why: Both are first-class. Minimal APIs suit small services and are faster to read; controllers earn their keep on large surfaces with cross-cutting filters and model binding conventions.

questions.q: How should long-running work be handled in a request?
choices: Queue it and return 202 Accepted with a way to check status; process it in a background service
Await it in the controller and increase the timeout
Use async void so the request returns immediately
Run it on a new Thread
questions.why: Holding a request open ties up resources and dies with the deploy. A hosted service reading from a queue survives restarts; fire-and-forget on a thread pool thread does not.

questions.q: What does `IHostedService` / `BackgroundService` give you?
choices: A long-running task with proper startup and graceful shutdown hooks, tied to the host lifetime
questions.why: It gets a CancellationToken on shutdown so it can finish cleanly. It is per instance though — scale to three replicas and your 'nightly job' runs three times unless you add a distributed lock.
questions.asked: The 'it runs on every instance' catch is the part that shows production experience.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in ASP.NET Core?
choices: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do
questions.why: UseAuthentication populates HttpContext.User from a cookie or token. UseAuthorization then evaluates policies and `[Authorize]` attributes. Registering them in the wrong order means every user looks anonymous.

questions.q: What is a claims-based identity?
choices: The user is represented as a set of claims (key/value assertions) that policies evaluate
A role name stored in the database
The username from the login form
questions.why: Roles are just one kind of claim. Policy-based authorization (`RequireClaim`, `RequireAssertion`) scales better than scattering role names through attributes.

questions.q: Why is `IMemoryCache` not enough once you scale out?
choices: Each instance has its own copy, so entries are inconsistent and invalidation does not propagate
It has a hard size limit
questions.why: Three instances, three caches, three different answers — and evicting on one does nothing to the others. A distributed cache (Redis) gives one shared view at the cost of a network hop.

questions.q: What does `WebApplicationFactory<T>` enable?
choices: Integration tests that boot the real app in memory and issue real HTTP requests, with services swappable
questions.why: It tests routing, model binding, middleware, filters and serialisation together — everything a unit test on a controller method misses. Usually paired with an in-memory or containerised database.

questions.q: How do you configure CORS correctly in ASP.NET Core?
choices: A named policy with explicit allowed origins, registered with UseCors before the endpoints
Add the header manually in each controller
questions.why: AllowAnyOrigin together with AllowCredentials is invalid and the browser rejects it — credentials require an explicit origin. And UseCors placed after the endpoints never sees the preflight.

questions.q: What does `services.AddHttpClient<T>()` solve?
choices: Socket exhaustion and stale DNS from manually constructing or statically holding HttpClient
questions.why: `new HttpClient()` per request leaks sockets in TIME_WAIT; one static instance never picks up DNS changes. The factory pools handlers and recycles them, and gives you a place to add Polly retry policies.
questions.asked: A well-known .NET gotcha that shows whether you have debugged a production networking issue.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Environment.IsDevelopment()` behaviour and production defaults?
choices: Development shows the developer exception page with stack traces; production must not
questions.why: A stack trace tells an attacker your framework versions, file paths and sometimes connection strings. `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` drives it, so getting that variable wrong in production is a real disclosure risk.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to return a 404 from a minimal API endpoint?
questions.why: TypedResults additionally gives a strongly typed return you can assert on in tests and that feeds OpenAPI metadata correctly.

questions.q: You add a field to an entity and the API stops returning existing rows correctly. Where do you look first?
choices: Whether a migration was created and applied to that environment's database
questions.why: Model and schema drift is the most common EF Core deployment failure. The general lesson: schema changes are deployments, and each environment has its own database state.
